TEST 1 · YOUR SAVINGS AND YOUR DIGNITY Digital arrest scams Article 21 · Life and personal liberty Fraudsters pose as police or judges and hold people on video calls until they transfer their savings. The Supreme Court took up the issue on its own in October 2025. → 29 Oct 2026: the Court said the RBI’s new rules must make banks compensate victims, at least the amount lost, where a failure of due diligence enabled the fraud. → WhatsApp and other platforms were asked to set out how they will prevent these scams. TEST 2 · WHAT YOU CAN READ Automated filters blocking the news Article 19(1)(a) · Speech and expression LiveLaw says its Instagram reels on Supreme Court hearings were restricted within about 15 minutes, with no order, notice or reasons. It has challenged Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, which requires platforms to filter content automatically. The constitutional question: Shreya Singhal (2015) upheld blocking because it came with reasons and a hearing. Can a mandatory filter skip both? Delhi HC, next hearing 18 January 2027. 5.4M+ ~41,000 META, INDIA PREVIOUS SIX MONTHS items restricted, Jan–Jun items restricted, Jul–Dec 2026 2025 Adv. TEST 3 · YOUR FACE IN PUBLIC Facial recognition at protests Article 21 · Privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017) The Supreme Court issued notice on 3 November 2026 on a petition asking whether police may use facial recognition on people at designated protest sites without a law authorising it. The constitutional question: Puttaswamy requires any intrusion on privacy to have a law behind it, a legitimate aim and proportionate means. Scanning every face at a protest site must pass that test. → The petition, by SFLC.in, is tagged with an earlier plea about the July 2026 Jantar Mantar protests. → The Union is yet to reply. No next date has been reported. Adv. Ashwani Kumar · kumarashwani-law.github.io 05 / 08

TEST 4 · WHO DECIDES ABOUT YOU AI in official decisions Article 14 · Equality and fair process → Telangana HC, 3 Nov 2026: suspended a Jangaon Collector’s land order said to have been passed ex parte with AI tools, without verifying facts. → Supreme Court, June 2026: draft rules propose a complete ban on AI deciding judicial outcomes. → CJI, 21 Nov 2026: no student should be found guilty of AI use on the word of a machine alone. THE GUARDIANS Articles 32 and 226 still work The CJI pointed to the writ powers of the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) as the protectors of fundamental rights. In tech cases, the route usually starts lower down: 1 Money lost to fraud: call 1930, file at cybercrime.gov.in, write to your bank, then the RBI Ombudsman. 2 Content or account blocked: appeal in the app, then the grievance officer, then the Grievance Appellate Committee. 3 State action without law or reasons: a writ petition in the High Court. MY TAKE The Constitution doesn’t need rewriting for AI. It needs applying. Dignity, equality, free speech and privacy were written for humans facing power.
